extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, statesmen, economists, and readers interested in public finance and tax design
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for designing public taxation (with emphasis on land taxes), aimed at producing equitable, certain, convenient, and minimally distortive revenue. Covers assessment methods, administrative safeguards, and specific treatments (leases, rents in kind, crown lands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution in proportion to ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of every state ought to contribute towards the support of the government, as nearly as possible, in proportion to their respective abilities; that is, in proportion to the revenue which they respectively enjoy under the protection of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim defines equality of taxation: individuals should pay according to the revenue they enjoy. The text notes that every tax that finally falls only on one of rent/profit/wages is necessarily unequal relative to the others, and that subsequent analysis will focus on inequality produced within the affected fund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of the tax (time, manner, quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tax which each individual is bound to pay, ought to be certain and not arbitrary. The time of payment, the manner of payment, the quantity to be paid, ought all to be clear and plain to the contributor, and to every other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certainty prevents extortion and corruption by tax collectors; the uncertainty of taxation encourages insolence and corruption among collectors and places contributors at their mercy. The author judges small uncertainty worse than considerable inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience of payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tax ought to be levied at the time, or in the manner, in which it is most likely to be convenient for the contributor to pay it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: land taxes payable when rents are usually paid; consumption taxes paid gradually as goods are bought. A tax convenient in timing and mode reduces hardship and likelihood of default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize extra burdens (collection costs and distortions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tax ought to be so contrived, as both to take out and to keep out of the pockets of the people as little as possible, over and above what it brings into the public treasury of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four ways taxes can be more burdensome than their yield: (1) expensive levying apparatus/officers and perquisites; (2) obstruction/discouragement of productive industry; (3) ruinous forfeitures and penalties from evasion attempts; (4) vexation/odious examinations by tax-gatherers. Design should minimize these wastes and distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax the fund that ultimately bears it
rubrics_metrics.description: All taxes, it is pretended, fall ultimately upon the rent of land, and ought, therefore, to be imposed equally upon the fund which must finally pay them. That all taxes ought to fall as equally as possible upon the fund which must finally pay them, is certainly true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical point used to motivate assessments: designers should understand which of rent/profit/wages ultimately bear a tax and attempt to impose taxes so that they fall equally on that final fund, though practical complications follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed (invariable) valuation method—certainty but aging unfairness
rubrics_metrics.description: A land tax assessed on each district according to a certain invariable canon (a fixed valuation) is perfectly certain and convenient, but necessarily becomes unequal over time as rents rise or fall in different districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed valuations are administratively cheap and certain, often payable at rent times; however, they can advantage or disadvantage landlords or the sovereign depending on long-term changes in rents or coin standard. A permanent constitution should suit all necessary circumstances, not transient ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable valuation method—equity and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon the rent of land which varies with every variation of the rent, or which rises and falls according to the improvement or neglect of cultivation, is recommended as the most equitable of all taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable taxes adapt to actual economic changes and share in improvements, but cost more to levy and may discourage improvements unless properly managed (see indemnification provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative recording of leases to ensure certainty and prevent fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The landlord and tenant might jointly be obliged to record their lease in a public register; proper penalties and informant incentives would deter concealment or misrepresentation of lease terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public register of leases (or similar administrative measures) can reduce uncertainty and expense in assessment, prevent collusion to defraud revenue, and make variable land taxes feasible without excessive administrative cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation treatment to discourage harmful landlord/tenant practices (lease-fines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking a fine for the renewal of the lease (selling future revenue for ready money) is generally hurtful to landlord, tenant, and community; by rendering such fines more heavily taxed than ordinary rent, the practice might be discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levying heavier tax on lease-fines discourages the conversion of future productive capital into immediate consumption that harms cultivation and long-term revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rents in kind or rent in service as additional rent and tax accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions in lease requiring certain modes of cultivation (rent in service) ought to be considered as an additional rent, 'a rent in service, instead of a rent in money,' and should be valued rather high and taxed somewhat higher than common money-rents; rents in kind are likewise more hurtful to tenants and should be discouraged by valuation/tax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher valuation/taxation of rents in kind or service discourages burdensome, anti-productive tenurial practices that impoverish tenants and lower overall produce and societal revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance/abatement for landlords who cultivate their own land (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the landlord chooses to occupy part of his own lands, the rent might be valued by equitable arbitration and a moderate abatement of tax granted to him, provided the rent of lands he occupies does not exceed a certain sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging landlords to cultivate part of their land can improve experimentation and improvements; but abatement should be limited so landlords are not tempted to farm the whole estate, which could degrade cultivation and harm the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-announced valuation/temporary rating to indemnify improvements under variable tax
rubrics_metrics.description: To obviate discouragement from a variable land-tax, allow the landlord, before improvement, to ascertain (with officers) the actual value and be rated according to this valuation for a number of years sufficient for his indemnification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The indemnification period should be long enough to compensate the landlord but not so long as to remoteness incentive; better somewhat too long than too short. This balances sovereign share in improvement with landlord incentives to invest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sale of unimproved crown lands and redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of the crown lands would produce a very large sum of money; when crown lands become private property they become improved and cultivated, increasing produce, population, and consequently customs/excise revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crown lands as unimproved wastes are socially costly; converting them to private property via sale often yields higher long-run public revenue and broader economic benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit crown ownership to pleasure/magnificence lands
rubrics_metrics.description: Lands for the purposes of pleasure and magnificence, parks, gardens, public walks, etc., seem to be the only lands which, in a great and civilized monarchy, ought to belong to the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aside from symbolic or ceremonial holdings, crown ownership of productive land is inefficient; productive lands should generally be private to maximize cultivation and societal revenue.
